result:
I’ve always believed that the best writing happens when you’re not writing *for* anything at all. No thesis, no agenda, no invisible audience holding a red pen. Just the pure pleasure of moving words around like stones in a river until something begins to sparkle. So here we are: 1000 words of pure drift.

The sky this morning was the color of a dove’s wing. Not poetic exaggeration; it really was that exact shade of soft, smoky lavender-gray that makes you forgive the world for being cold. I stood on the porch with coffee that was already going lukewarm and watched a single crow bully three sparrows out of the bird feeder. The crow didn’t even eat much. It just wanted them to know who was in charge. There’s a lesson in that somewhere about power, but I don’t feel like extracting it today. Sometimes a crow is just an asshole with feathers.

I’ve been thinking lately about how much of life is spent managing the gap between what we imagined and what actually shows up. We build these beautiful mental dioramas, complete with lighting and soundtracks, and then reality arrives like a tired postal worker who’s been delivering the wrong package to the wrong address for twenty years. The trick, I’m learning (slowly, painfully, the way one learns everything worth knowing), is to keep the diorama but stop expecting it to become the house you actually live in. Keep the dream. Just don’t try to move furniture into it.

There’s a Japanese concept called *wabi-sabi* that I keep coming back to like a tongue to a missing tooth. The beauty of imperfection. The melancholy loveliness of things that are incomplete, transient, a little broken. A chipped teacup that somehow makes the tea taste better. The way an old wooden floor creaks in exactly the right places so you never have to turn the lights on at night; your feet already know the song. We spend so much energy trying to make things permanent and flawless when the universe is clearly running on a different operating system. Entropy is not a bug. It’s the central feature.

I’ve started talking to my houseplants. Not in the cute Instagram way where people coo at monstera leaves. I have full conversations with them, usually after midnight when the rest of the world has the decency to be quiet. I tell the rubber plant about my money anxieties. The snake plant gets updates on my love life (or lack thereof). The pathetic little pothos that somehow refuses to die despite my criminal neglect hears about my fears that I’m wasting my life. They never interrupt. They never offer solutions. They just sit there being green and alive and somehow that’s enough. Maybe that’s all any of us really need; someone who will witness us without trying to fix us.

There’s a saxophone player who busks near the train station every Thursday. He’s terrible. Gloriously, unapologetically terrible. He plays “Careless Whisper” like he’s strangling a goose, and yet I find myself dropping money in his case every single time. Not out of pity. There’s something courageous about being that bad at something in public. Most of us are mediocre at best at the things we do, but we hide it behind closed doors, behind carefully curated social media feeds, behind ironic detachment. This guy just stands in the cold with his terrible saxophone and his terrible playing and dares the world to look at him. I respect that. I want to be that brave about my own mediocrity.

Yesterday I found an old notebook from when I was twenty-two. The handwriting looks like it belongs to a completely different person; all sharp angles and certainty. The pages are filled with grand pronouncements about art and truth and how the world needs to be saved by beautiful sentences. I read it with the mixture of tenderness and embarrassment you feel when watching old videos of yourself dancing. Who was that boy? So arrogant. So convinced that he was special. So certain that the universe owed him an audience.

I don’t know if I’ve become wiser or just more tired. Probably both. The arrogance has mostly burned off, leaving something smaller but maybe more durable. I still believe in beautiful sentences. I just no longer think they’ll save anyone, least of all me. They’re more like little paper boats you set on the river. Most of them sink. A few might make it around the bend where you can’t see anymore. That has to be enough.

I keep six different houseplants alive (barely) but can’t keep a single houseplant of a relationship alive for more than two seasons. There’s probably a metaphor there but I’m too close to it to see clearly. People are not plants. They need different things. They need to be seen in all their seasons, not just when they’re putting out new growth. They need you to stay when they go dormant instead of assuming they’re dead and throwing them away. I’m still learning that one. The plants are better teachers than they realize.

Sometimes I fantasize about disappearing. Not in a dark way; just packing a small bag, taking the train to somewhere I’ve never been, and starting over with a different name. I’d be a quiet person who works in a bookstore and reads too much and never tells anyone about the years I spent trying to become a writer. I’d grow a terrible beard and learn to make perfect espresso and maybe, finally, be at peace with being ordinary. Then I remember that I’d probably just take all my neuroses with me on the train, and they’d be waiting for me when I stepped off at the new station, tapping their feet impatiently like “Took you long enough.”

The truth is I don’t want to disappear. I want to become more visible in the right ways. I want to write the things I’m actually afraid to write. I want to love people with the kind of love that doesn’t keep score. I want to get better at being alive instead of just performing aliveness for various audiences.

The dove-colored sky has turned into proper rain now. The kind that sounds like static on an old radio. My coffee is completely cold. The crow is gone, probably off somewhere counting his victories. The plants are still quietly photosynthesizing, doing their slow green work without complaint. The saxophone player is probably at home practicing, though I hope not. Some things are perfect in their imperfection.

I’ve written almost exactly a thousand words now. None of it was planned. None of it will change the world. But for a little while, the river of words moved smoothly and the stones caught the light just so. That feels like enough.

And somewhere, a rubber plant is wondering why I haven’t told it about my dreams lately. I should probably go do that. The night is young, the plants are listening, and the rain keeps excellent rhythm.
